business_ops.seasonality: The Company's renewable energy projects generate revenue as a direct function of the electricity they generate, which is influenced significantly by environmental conditions, irradiation and wind speed. Power generation is highly dependent on weather conditions, and profitability depends not only on observed weather conditions at the project site but also on the consistency of those conditions. Operating results for renewable energy projects vary depending on natural variations from season to season and from year to year, and may also change permanently because of climate change or other factors beyond the Company's control. Electricity output is partially dependent on sunlight/irradiation or wind speed, and generation may decrease under certain environmental conditions including cloudy weather, sandstorms, heavy rainfall, solar eclipses and environmental pollution. The Company engages in regular O&M of its Operational Projects and cleaning of solar modules to minimise the impact of soiling, but cannot assure that such initiatives will offset environmental conditions. The seasonal nature of its energy production can also place additional demands on working capital reserves and borrowing capacity under existing debt, particularly during periods when cash flow from operations is reduced.

business_ops.supply_chain_integration: The Company manages the end-to-end lifecycle of renewable energy project development in-house across all critical stages: (i) bidding and auction; (ii) site prospecting; (iii) land acquisition and grid permits; (iv) engineering and technology; (v) procurement; (vi) project financing; (vii) plant construction and commissioning; and (viii) O&M. It adopts a selective and strategic approach to auctions backed by regulatory and commercial analysis, and identifies high-potential sites using GIS tools, irradiance datasets and wind resource assessments. A dedicated project development team has built a substantial land bank (more than 12,000 acres for solar and more than 300 WTG locations across Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh) and the business development team has secured surplus grid connectivity beyond that allocated to all Under Construction Projects as at June 30, 2026. Engineering and technology design is handled internally by specialists covering layout, balance of plant, turbine technology and battery storage systems. Procurement is managed through long-term relationships and advance orders with global suppliers. By integrating EPC and O&M functions in-house, the Company retains construction margins typically passed to third-party contractors, which it states enhances control over timelines, cost and quality, enables competitive bids and higher profitability, and allows project designs and technology choices to be tailored to site requirements. Operational Projects have been commissioned ahead of schedule by a weighted average of 147 days, with one solar Operational Project commencing 552 days ahead of schedule and one wind Operational Project 222 days ahead of schedule on a weighted average basis. Strategic long-term supply partnerships as at June 30, 2026 include a WTG supply agreement with Envision, a wind operated electricity generator (WOEG) supply agreement with Suzlon Energy Limited, solar module tie-ups with First Solar (for around 1.60 years), Waaree (for around 2.20 years) and Goldi (for around 2.20 years), inverter supply from Sungrow (India) Private Limited, SVGs tie-up with TBEA Xi'an Electric Technology Co. Ltd. and BESS with Envision. Key Managerial Personnel and Senior Management are supported by more than 700 employees working across the projects as at June 30, 2026. The Company is dependent on suppliers for critical components: its top 10 suppliers contributed 84.42%, 79.99% and 87.52% of total purchases for Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024 respectively; key components are wind turbine generators for wind projects and solar modules and inverters for solar projects; procurement agreements typically require manufacturers to provide warranties against equipment failures and defects for a specified period. Other than as disclosed in the risk factor on price changes in solar modules, wind turbines, inverters and other materials, the Company states it has not faced significant disruptions in the procurement of critical components in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024.

strategy_growth.detail: Growth depends on securing rights to sites suitable for development, determined by cost, solar radiation, wind, grid connection infrastructure and other factors. Securing land rights involves complex negotiations with multiple landowners and local communities for rights-of-way; some Under Construction Contracted and Awarded Projects are in remote areas. Land parcels may not be contiguous due to litigation, sand dunes, water channels/bodies, railway tracks, high transmission lines, forest land, revenue issues and landowner unwillingness. Failure could result in liquidated damages under PPAs and tariff reductions if commissioning deadlines are missed.

A SEBI complaint from the same former Chief Executive Officer alleging the Company engaged in coercion, bribery and unethical practices; the Audit Committee conducted an independent investigation and the Company replied on September 26, 2025 that the allegations are false, wholly untenable and devoid of merit. The Complaint and Response are annexed to the RHP and published on the Company website until the Bid/Issue Closing Date.

Litigation load is large relative to earnings: aggregate disclosed litigation of Rs 34,316.2 lakhs equals 848.07% of restated PAT and 10.02% of net worth, and no provisions had been made for possible liabilities arising out of pending litigations as at March 31, 2026. The materiality threshold itself is set at Rs 19.50 mn, the lowest of 2% of turnover (Rs 143.79 mn), 2% of net worth (Rs 684.78 mn) and 5% of average absolute PAT (Rs 19.50 mn).

Statutory auditor remarks under Rule 11(g) in all three fiscals: the audit trail feature was not enabled at the database level for the accounting software to log direct data changes in FY2024 and FY2025, and was enabled only from March 21, 2026 for FY2026, with similar remarks by subsidiary auditors.

The RHP states plainly that 'Presently we do not have any defined policy to address this conflict of interest', while certain Subsidiaries are authorised under their memorandums to develop, own and operate utility-scale renewable energy projects and Promoter Group members may compete with the business.

A 10-for-1 bonus issue of 444,535,720 Equity Shares on March 26, 2025 — roughly 16 months before the RHP and 13 days after the last cash rights issue at Rs 1,163.84 per share on March 13, 2025 — leaves the Corporate Promoter's certified average cost of acquisition at Rs 67.20 per Equity Share.

Three projects sat past their Scheduled Commercial Operation Date and uncommissioned as at June 30, 2026, with extension petitions pending on force majeure grounds, after liquidated damages of Rs 3.73 mn, Rs 5.30 mn, Rs 22.43 mn and Rs 67.20 mn across four projects, three of them paid under protest.

Governance record defects surfaced in extraction: a related-party note dates a subsidiary's inclusion '31 February 2025', a date that does not exist; the AT Holdings Pte. Ltd. board table numbers rows 1, 2, 4 and 5 with serial 3 absent; and Sanjay Kumar Bakliwal appears as a Non-Executive Director in the Key Managerial Personnel list of the Restated Consolidated Financial Information with no cessation date, while Risk Factor 48 states he resigned on July 3, 2026 and he is not among the eight Directors on the Board at the RHP date.

Delays in payment of statutory dues in all three fiscals — TDS/TCS in 4, 14 and 40 instances (interest Rs 0.03 / 0.19 / 0.36 mn), advance tax in 16 and 18 instances (Rs 1.97 / 3.04 mn), plus GST, provident fund, labour welfare fund and professional tax instances — together with penalties for delayed creation of security interests at Juniper Green Three (5 days, Rs 0.99 mn), Sigma (14 days, Rs 0.16 mn), Nisagra (74 days, Rs 2.84 mn) and the Company itself (35 days, Rs 0.64 mn).

A portion of the Net Proceeds will repay the Rs 40,000.0 lakhs green loan from The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, an affiliate of Book Running Lead Manager HSBC Securities and Capital Markets (India) Private Limited; the RHP states there is no conflict of interest under Regulation 21A but acknowledges the arrangement may be perceived as one.

An outstanding regulatory proceeding against subsidiary Nisagra Renewable Energy Private Limited over a 10.00 MW solar project at Nashik, Maharashtra, with the adverse-decision amount stated as not quantifiable; separately, income-tax scrutiny notices for AY 2025-26 on the Company and seven Subsidiaries are excluded from the litigation summary table because those assessments are incomplete.
strengths_observed: Contracted revenue base is long-dated and investment-grade: as at June 30, 2026, 97.68% of Total Capacity (MWp) is backed by long-term PPAs, typically 25 years (only Juniper Green Ray Two's PPA is 20 years), with counterparties rated "A" or above; the RHP states no PPA was terminated in Fiscals 2026, 2025 or 2024. Average portfolio tariff Rs 3.64/kWh (FY26), Rs 3.63 (FY25), Rs 3.41 (FY24).

Operating scale compounded fast: revenue from operations Rs 3,915.50 mn (FY24) to Rs 5,086.78 mn (FY25) to Rs 7,189.34 mn (FY26); EBITDA Rs 37,084.3 lakhs to Rs 48,568.5 lakhs to Rs 69,218.4 lakhs; operational installed AC capacity 660.20 MW (FY24) to 1,324.20 MW (FY26) and 1,794.80 MW as at June 30, 2026 across 20 projects.

Asset uptime is high and improving across all three fiscals: Average Grid Availability 99.40% / 99.31% / 99.12% and Average Plant Availability 99.16% / 98.81% / 98.57% for FY26 / FY25 / FY24; average Capacity Utilization Factor 24.99% / 26.03% / 25.83%.

Demonstrated ability to build early on the legacy solar/wind book: Operational Projects were commissioned ahead of schedule by a weighted average of 147 days across 977.15 MW AC (1,304.24 MWp DC), with one solar project 552 days and one wind project 222 days ahead on a weighted average basis.

Positioning per the commissioned CRISIL Report: among the top 10 largest renewable IPPs in India by Total Capacity as at March 31, 2026, and second largest bidder by total capacity won in WSH and FDRE tenders concluded between April 1, 2021 and March 31, 2026, with a 96.80% conversion rate on tenders won in that period.

Credit standing has not deteriorated through the leverage build: ICRA long-term/short-term ratings A+ (Positive)/A1 in Fiscal 2026 and A+ (Stable)/A1 in Fiscals 2025 and 2024, with no downgrades in any of the three fiscals.

Development runway already secured: land bank of more than 12,000 acres for solar and more than 300 WTG locations across Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, plus grid connectivity surplus to all Under Construction Projects as at June 30, 2026 — against the CRISIL Report's statement that a developer applying for connectivity today in Rajasthan/Gujarat may not obtain it until Fiscal 2030.

Collection discipline on a Discom-heavy book: trade receivable days 23.06 (FY24), 16.94 (FY25), 21.88 (FY26); trade receivables 6.23% / 4.54% / 5.82% of revenue from operations; receivables outstanding over one year of only Rs 19.4 lakhs at March 31, 2026, equal to 0.01% of net worth.
Free (unpledged) cash of Rs 24,787.65 mn at March 31, 2026 after DSRA pledges of Rs 1,344.21 mn and LC/BG margin of Rs 8,749.66 mn, up from Rs 11,331.33 mn (FY25) and Rs 4,585.74 mn (FY24).

End-to-end in-house model (bidding, land, grid, engineering, procurement, EPC and O&M) which the RHP states retains construction margins otherwise passed to third-party contractors; equipment secured through long-term tie-ups with Envision (1 GW of 5.00 MW EN 182 WTGs), Suzlon, First Solar, Waaree, Goldi, Sungrow and TBEA.
